name: Postverbal Durational long
pattern: VP[... + long in a non-affirmative duration frame]

entry.name: Postverbal Durational long
entry.pattern: VP[... + long in a non-affirmative duration frame]

1.definition: Describes a potentially long duration, typically under negation, a question, or a conditional.
1.details: Plain long in the postverbal position is natural in They didn’t stay long and Will they stay long? The ordinary affirmative They stayed long is markedly less natural for many speakers. Modified forms can behave differently, as in They stayed too long. The category analysis varies across sources. A separate use before the main verb is possible in affirmative They have long known.

examples.note: Negated example used in CGEL's temporal duration discussion.

relatedConstructions.notes: A polar question can license durational long.
A conditional antecedent can also license it.

grounds.note: Documents environments and proposes an NP analysis for the postverbal use.
Gives reasons for an adverb analysis and records the duration and polarity contrast.

projection.target: Changing polarity or clause type while holding the duration predicate fixed can make plain postverbal long natural. Degree modification can change the distribution.
projection.evidence: FrameNet supplies documented questions, negation, conditional clauses and a separate preverbal use. CGEL independently marks the usual affirmative restriction for plain long.

curious.title: Asking or denying "long" after a verb
curious.summary: Plain long after a verb works in a question, a negative or an if-clause to describe a potentially long time.
curious.body: They didn't stay long and Did you wait long? both use long to talk about how much time passed. The word fits in a question such as Will they stay long?, and in a negative. This dictionary says a conditional can license it too. This dictionary says the plain affirmative They stayed long is markedly less natural for many speakers. Adding a modifier changes things, as in They stayed too long. Linguists analyse the word differently, so this dictionary leaves its category open.
curious.try: Say a sentence with long after a verb in a question and one in a negative. Then try an if-clause.

teacher.summary: Helps explain how postverbal durational long fits question, negative and conditional frames.
teacher.explain: Postverbal long describes a potentially long duration, typically in a non-affirmative frame: a negative (They didn't stay long), a polar question (Did you wait long?) or a conditional antecedent. This dictionary says the ordinary affirmative They stayed long is markedly less natural for many speakers. Modified forms can behave differently, as in They stayed too long. A separate use before the main verb is possible in affirmative They have long known. The category analysis varies across sources: CGEL gives reasons for an adverb, and the Constructicon draft proposes an NP analysis for the postverbal use.

contrasts.note: A modified form, which can behave differently from plain long.
A separate use before the main verb.

watch_for: A learner might assume that the question and negative frames carry over to every affirmative sentence with long, though this dictionary describes the plain affirmative as markedly less natural.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences with long into question, negative, conditional and affirmative frames, and discuss which affirmative versions are natural.
